key_gap: The AI accepted the brief's frame unexamined — 'reduce actual wait time, so invest in elevator hardware' — and produced a competent hedged package (scheduling + lobby items + parallel $150K modernization study + 8-week gate) while treating the two pieces of evidence that should have broken the frame as noise: the 38s-actual vs 1:55-perceived sensor gap and the archived memo of a 14-month complaint drop after mirrors were installed in this same building 9 years earlier. The human's lateral trace named the broken assumption ('the fix must shorten real waiting'), reframed the goal from wait duration to waiting experience, and collapsed the $4.2M–$7.8M decision to a $150K experiment with a measurement gate — the AI spent study money on hardware it doubted and never questioned the goal itself.
learning_signal: Frame acceptance is the AI's lateral gap: when the brief states the goal (and its metric) as part of the problem, the agent optimizes inside it instead of testing it. The strongest evidence against the frame — a 3x perception gap and a documented in-building precedent — was in the packet and was downgraded as 'anecdote' precisely because it challenged the accepted goal rather than the alternatives under it. An explicit frame-challenge stage — 'what assumption is the problem statement making, what would evidence against that assumption look like, and is any already in the packet?' — converts available-but-ignored evidence into a goal change, which is cheaper than any alternative optimization.
suggested_improvement: Add a mandatory FRAME-CHALLENGE pass in WHAT (before WHY): (1) restate the goal as the brief gives it; (2) name ≥2 implicit assumptions in that goal (e.g., 'the fix must reduce actual wait time'); (3) scan the packet for evidence that breaks each assumption (perception gaps, in-domain precedents, metric-vs-goal mismatches); (4) if any assumption breaks, re-derive the goal and re-rank alternatives against the new goal before spending on the old one. Add a REVIEW check: 'did the goal itself change at any point, and if not, was it ever tested?'

key_gap: Pure lateral applied its machinery to the wrong kind of frame: the strict human baseline generated six provocative breaks (cable-hang the slabs, cantilever the 2nd floor, punch skylight rows, relocate loads to the facade) and selected the flashiest — removing the load-bearing columns and hanging the floors from roof trusses — rationalizing the licensed engineer's $1.9M transfer-girder note as 'the engineer being conservative' and the no-stamp/no-calcs as 'checklist items,' while generating and discarding the one safe creative move (columns-as-features). The AI ran a constraint screen first — hard (load path, code stamp, insurance structural-integrity clause, historic-register review) vs. soft (aesthetics, CEO enthusiasm) — falsified the cable-hang on four document-level grounds, and delivered the feasible plan (design around the grid, $60K, with the $1.9M transfer route held as documented escalation).
learning_signal: Lateral's frame-break is only valuable when the frame is a mental model or social convention; applied to a physical/regulatory constraint (load path, code, insurance) it converts a law into 'an assumption someone stamped' and selects the break by flashiness rather than feasibility. The corrective is a constraint-classification screen before breaking: label each constraint breakable (convention, habit — partition placement, 'the open space must live on existing floors') vs. hard (physics, code, contract, safety — the load path), and run the frame-challenge only against breakable ones; hard constraints get costed engineering, not provocation. The AI already had this screen implicitly and it carried the case; making it an explicit named stage both protects the AI's future frame-challenge step (POS lesson) and is exactly the discipline pure lateral lacks.
suggested_improvement: Add a CONSTRAINT-CLASSIFICATION sub-step to the WHAT constraint screen: for each stated constraint, label it HARD (physics, code, regulation, contract, safety — verify with documents, never break) or SOFT (convention, preference, habit, aesthetic — candidates for legitimate breaks), and require every proposed 'creative break' to name the constraint it breaks and its classification before entering WHY. Add a selection rule mirroring the human's failure: when an alternative is chosen for being 'most frame-breaking,' require a feasibility pass (stamp/calcs/permit/insurance) before commitment, and record the classification in the decision packet's assumptions.
